description: A team of young engineers gathered to solve one space challenge and have fun along the way
summary:
SONATA (Earth Information Jukebox) is a web app that turns NASA’s ECCO2 ocean model data into music, so people can hear the ocean instead of only looking at it. Each ocean metric is mapped to its own instrument, and users can toggle instruments on and off to hear how different measurements change across place and time.

It addresses the challenge by making complex Earth data approachable through sound. A scientific mode keeps the audio faithful to the data. A separate fun mode allows freer tuning and instruments, and lets users bring in their own musical taste. Users can choose a location and share what they hear as a short clip.

It matters because most ocean data is locked behind charts and maps. SONATA treats visually impaired users as a primary audience, with keyboard and screen reader access, a live data readout, audio cues, panning, and text equivalents, and it passes accessibility checks with zero violations. Sound makes ocean change easier to understand for everyone.
details:
What it does and how it works

SONATA turns NASA’s ECCO2 ocean model data into sound. Each ocean metric [confirm which, e.g. temperature, salinity, currents, sea surface height] is mapped to its own instrument, and users can toggle instruments on and off to hear how different measurements change across place and time. A scientific mode keeps the audio faithful to the data. A separate fun mode allows freer tuning and instrument choices, and lets users select or import music they like to shape the output. Users can pick a location, hear its ocean data, and share the result as a clip, card, or animation.

Benefits

  • Makes dense ocean data easier to grasp by ear, without needing to read charts or maps.
  • Works for curious people with no science background and for visually impaired users.
  • Lets people connect to ocean change in a personal way, through a place they know or music they like.
  • Gives everyone a shareable output, so the data spreads beyond the app.

Intended impact

We want more people to engage with NASA ocean data and understand what it says about a changing planet. Treating visually impaired users as a primary audience widens who can access this data at all. A clip someone can send to a friend turns a single visit into a conversation about the ocean and climate.

Tools and technology

  • Data: NASA’s ECCO2 ocean model
  • Development: mostly AI-assisted (vibe-coded), starting once the UI/UX design was ready
  • Hosting: sonata.manus.space
  • Accessibility testing: axe-core, with 0 violations on the latest checkpoint
  • [Add framework, language, and audio engine, e.g. Web Audio API, if that is what you used]
  • [Add the design and video tools used by the UI/UX and motion graphics members]

Creativity

  • Sonification of a global ocean model, with one instrument per metric that users can mix like a band.
  • Two modes, so scientific accuracy and playful exploration each get what they need.
  • “Local” works at two levels: local to a place and local to a person’s own musical taste.
  • Accessibility is built into the core experience through keyboard and screen reader access, a live readout, audio cues, panning, and text equivalents.

Factors the team considered

  • Audience: a core experience for curious people first, with visually impaired users as a second priority but a primary group.
  • Scientific integrity: culture and personal taste must never distort the data-driven audio, which is why they live only in fun mode. We dropped the maqam idea for this reason and because judges may not be invested in Arabic music.
  • Team skills: we have no musician, so the design had to work without deep musical expertise.
  • Scope and time: we restarted the core engine from scratch to get a presentable demo on a clear dataset within the hackathon window.
